'''Catherine Clarke Fenselau''' (born 15 April 1939) is an American scientist who was the first trained [[Mass spectrometry|mass spectrometrist]] on the faculty of an American medical school; she joined [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]] in 1968.<ref name=Rapid /><ref name=Kaltashov>{{cite journal|last1=Kaltashov|first1=Igor A.|first2=Richard B. |last2= van Breemen|title=Special issue honoring Catherine Fenselau|journal=International Journal of Mass Spectrometry|date=15 February 2012|volume=312|pages=1–4|doi=10.1016/j.ijms.2012.01.014|bibcode=2012IJMSp.312....1K|author1-link=Igor Kaltashov}}</ref><ref name=Shearer>{{cite book|editor-last=Shearer|editor-first=Benjamin F.|editor2-last=Shearer|editor2-first=Barbara Smith|title=Notable women in the physical sciences: a biographical dictionary|year=1997|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, Conn.|isbn=978-0313293030|edition=1st|page=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780313293030/page/97 97]|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780313293030/page/97}}</ref> She specializes in biomedical applications of mass spectrometry.<ref name=Oakes>{{cite book|last=Oakes|first=Elizabeth H.|title=Encyclopedia of world scientists|year=2007|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York|isbn=9781438118826|pages=228–229|edition=Rev.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&pg=PA228}}</ref> She has been recognized as an outstanding scientist in the field of bioanalytical chemistry because of her work using mass spectrometry to study biomolecules.<ref name="Adams" />

==Early life and education==
Catherine Lee Clarke was born on 15 April 1939, in [[York, Nebraska]].<ref name=Oakes /><ref name=Interview>{{cite web|title=Catherine Fenselau, Her Life and Career in Science|url=https://www.ushupo.org/About/USHUPONews/Vol4,Winter2013/MemberProfiles/tabid/165/Default.aspx|publisher=US HUPO|accessdate=16 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140325210917/https://www.ushupo.org/About/USHUPONews/Vol4,Winter2013/MemberProfiles/tabid/165/Default.aspx|archive-date=25 March 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> She graduated from [[Bryn Mawr College]] in 1961 with an [[Artium baccalaureus]] in chemistry.<ref name=Oakes />

She received a Ph.D. in [[organic chemistry]] in 1965 from [[Stanford University]], working with [[Carl Djerassi]].<ref name=Oakes /> As a field, organic mass spectrometry was new and had great potential impact for the pharmaceutical industry. The mass spectrometer was a new tool for examining the structures of small botanical molecules. Djerassi's lab examined electron ionization of molecules, studying basic mechanisms such as fragmentation and hydrogen transfer. For her thesis research, Catherine made a series of deuterium labeled analogues of amines, alcohols, esters and amides.<ref name=Interview />

== Career ==
She spent the next two years in postdoctoral positions, studying on a 1965–1966 fellowship from the [[American Association of University Women]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] with [[Melvin Calvin]]. In 1967, she worked at the [[Space Sciences Laboratory]] with Melvin Calvin and A. L. Burlingame.<ref name="CV" /> Calvin's lab was developing methods to be used in the analysis of lunar rock samples. Fenselau described an analysis technique for preparing lipid samples from [[Moon rocks]], before actual lunar samples were available for testing.<ref name="Interview" />

=== Johns Hopkins School of Medicine ===
Fenselau was the first trained mass spectroscopist to join a medical faculty when she joined the mass spectrometry laboratory in the Pharmacology Department at [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine|Johns Hopkins University]] in 1968.<ref name="Rapid">{{cite journal|title=Mass Spectrometry at Johns Hopkins and the University of Maryland Baltimore County|journal=Rapid Communications in Mass Spectrometry|year=1994|volume=8|issue=9|pages=763–765|doi=10.1002/rcm.1290080921|bibcode=1994RCMS....8..763.|doi-access=free}}</ref> When she arrived, Johns Hopkins did not have a mass spectrometer. Fenselau did her initial research by driving to the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) laboratories to use their instruments. [[Paul Talalay]], chairman of Pharmacology, and [[Albert L. Lehninger]], the chairman of Biological Chemistry, submitted proposals for funding for a state of the art mass spectrometer. They were successful in obtaining funding from the [[National Science Foundation]] for a CEC 21-110 double-focusing mass spectrometer for Fenselau to use.<ref name="Rapid" /><ref name="Interview" />

She has done considerable work in the area of cancer and anti-cancer treatments, studying drugs such as [[cyclophosphamide]]. With oncologist O. M. Colvin,<!-- O. Michael Colvin --> she identified the active metabolite of cyclophosphamide, and published the first quantification of the drug and its metabolites in urine and blood from patients.<ref name="Interview" /> She led the development of synthetic and analytical methods for glucuronides, and studied the reactions of acyl-linked glucuronides with Martin Stogniew, work that has been important in understanding drug-derived liver disease.<ref name="Rapid" /><ref name="Stogniew">{{cite journal|last=Stogniew|first=M|author2=Fenselau, C|title=Electrophilic reactions of acyl-linked glucuronides. Formation of clofibrate mercapturate in humans.|journal=Drug Metabolism and Disposition|date=Nov–Dec 1982|volume=10|issue=6|pages=609–13|pmid=6130909}}</ref>

=== University of Maryland ===
Although Fenselau and her second husband Robert Cotter both worked in mass spectrometry at Johns Hopkins, they chose to develop independent careers rather than a joint lab. "We felt that we could make twice as many contributions to science if we had two separate labs and evolved in our own ways that reflected our own skills and our own institutions."<ref name="Interview" />

In 1987, Catherine Fenselau moved to the [[University of Maryland, Baltimore County]] (UMBC) to become chairperson of the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry.<ref name="Rapid" /> She chose the university in part because she wanted greater opportunities for teaching. At UMBC she was one of the first faculty members involved in the [[Meyerhoff Scholarship Program]], an initiative of UMBC president [[Freeman Hrabowski]] to attract minority undergraduate researchers.<ref name="Interview" />

There, funding from the [[National Institutes of Health]], the [[National Science Foundation]], and others enabled Fenselau to establish a state-of-the-art mass spectrometry lab, the Structural Biochemistry Center (SBC). Equipment included a JEOL HX110/110 four-sector tandem mass spectrometer, a Hewlett-Packard quadrupole mass spectrometer with particle beam and Vestec electrospray ion sources, and 500 and 600&nbsp;MHz NMR spectrometers. Research areas studied in the lab included [[biopolymer]] structure, ion [[thermochemistry]], proton-binding entropies, [[glucuronide]] and [[glutathione]] conjugation, and possible mechanisms for acquired [[drug resistance]].<ref name="Rapid" />

In June 1987, Fenselau oversaw the installation of a HighResMALDI [[Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance|Fourier transform mass spectrometer]] in her lab. The Fourier transform mass spectrometer used a strong magnetic field to trap and excite ions and measure the resulting electrical signals. Appointed Chairperson of the Department of Chemistry at [[University of Maryland, College Park]] in 1998, Fenselau supervised the disassembly, transport, and reassembly of the complex instrument, moving it safely to her new lab.<ref name="Oakes" /> With it, she has studied the chemistry of gaseous ions, chemical reactions of drugs with proteins, and [[posttranslational modification]] in protein biosynthesis.<ref name="Oakes" />

In 2005, she acted as the interim Dean for the College of Graduate Studies and Associate Vice President for Research in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry,<ref name="Oakes" /> and was named Distinguished University Professor at the University of Maryland in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Two Named 2017 Distinguished University Professors in College of Computer, Mathematical, and Natural Sciences {{!}} College of Computer, Mathematical, and Natural Sciences {{!}} University of Maryland |url=https://cmns.umd.edu/news-events/news/two-named-2017-distinguished-university-professors-college-computer-mathematical |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=cmns.umd.edu}}</ref> She has been president of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry (ASMS) from 1982 to 1984, founding president of US-Human Proteome Organization (US HUPO), and senior vice president of international Human Proteome Organization.<ref name="Kaltashov" /> She serves as a member of the Western Region of the Awards Committee of the Human Proteome Organization.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HUPO - Committees |url=https://www.hupo.org/HUPO-Committees |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=www.hupo.org}}</ref>

She was the founding editor of ''Biomedical Mass Spectrometry'' (now the ''Journal of Mass Spectrometry'') and associate editor of ''Analytical Chemistry''.<ref name="Kaltashov" /> She has published more than 350 peer-reviewed articles.<ref name="Kaltashov" /> A 2020 issue of the Journal of Mass Spectrometry is dedicated to Fenselau for her distinguished career.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van Breemen |first1=Richard B. |last2=Hathout |first2=Yetrib |last3=Fabris |first3=Dan |date=2020 |title=SPECIAL ISSUE TITLE: Special issue dedicated to Catherine Fenselau |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jms.4391 |journal=Journal of Mass Spectrometry |language=en |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=ii |doi=10.1002/jms.4391|bibcode=2020JMSp...55D...2V |s2cid=213405493 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

Catherine Fenselau continues to teach at the University of Maryland College Park. More than 150 post-doctoral fellows, graduate students and undergraduate students have received training in her laboratories at [[Johns Hopkins University]], [[University of Maryland, Baltimore County]], and the [[University of Maryland, College Park]].<ref name="CV" />

==Awards==
Fenselau has received a number of significant awards, including the following.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Catherine Fenselau|url=http://www.chem.umd.edu/catherine-fenselau/|publisher=University of Maryland|accessdate=16 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161029220141/http://www.chem.umd.edu/catherine-fenselau|archive-date=29 October 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>  
* [[Garvan–Olin Medal|Garvan Medal]], 1985 as a distinguished woman in chemistry.<ref name=Garvan>{{cite web|title=Francis P. Garvan-John M. Olin Medal|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/francis-p-garvan-john-m-olin-medal.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=16 March 2014}}</ref> 
* Maryland Chemist of the Year, [[American Chemical Society]], 1989.<ref name=MarylandChemist>{{cite web|title=Maryland Chemist Award|url=http://maryland.sites.acs.org/marylandchemistaward.htm|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=16 March 2014|archive-date=24 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140224215357/http://maryland.sites.acs.org/marylandchemistaward.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> 
* Eastern Analytical Symposium Award for Outstanding Achievements in the Fields of Analytical Chemistry, 1999<ref>{{Cite web |title=Previous EAS Award Recipients |url=https://eas.org/?page_id=8566 |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=EAS 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref> 
* [[National Institutes of Health MERIT Award]], 1991–2001.<ref name="Oakes" />
* Distinguished Service Award, Human Proteome Organization, 2006<ref>{{Cite web |title=HUPO - Past Award Recipients |url=https://www.hupo.org/Past-Award-Recipients |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=www.hupo.org |archive-date=2022-12-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221227160158/https://www.hupo.org/Past-Award-Recipients |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* Field & Franklin Award for Contributions in Mass spectrometry, American Chemical Society (ACS), 2008.<ref name=Field>{{cite web|title=Frank H. Field and Joe L. Franklin Award for Outstanding Achievement in Mass Spectrometry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/frank-h-field-and-joe-l-franklin-award-for-outstanding-achievement-in-mass-spectrometry.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=20 March 2014}}</ref> 
* Thomson Medal, International Mass Spectrometry Foundation, 2009.<ref name=Thomson>{{cite web|title=The 2014 Thomson Medal Award|url=http://www.imsc2014.ch/?page_id=46|publisher=International Mass Spectrometry Foundation|accessdate=20 March 2014|archive-date=25 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140325210238/http://www.imsc2014.ch/?page_id=46|url-status=dead}}</ref> 
* Ralph N. Adams Award in Bioanalytical Chemistry, 2010 <ref name=Adams>{{cite news|last=Brown|first=Steve|title=Ralph N. Adams Award|url=http://www.chromatographyonline.com/lcgc/Ralph-N-Adams-Award/ArticleStandard/Article/detail/658915|accessdate=20 March 2014|newspaper=Spectroscopy Wavelength|date=2 March 2010}}</ref> 
* John B. Fenn Award for a Distinguished Contribution in Mass Spectrometry, American Society for Mass Spectrometry, 2012.<ref name=Edwards>{{cite journal|last=Edwards|first=Nathan J.|author2=Bierbaum, Veronica M.|title=Focus in Honor of Dr. Catherine Fenselau, Recipient of the 2012 Award for a Distinguished Contribution in Mass Spectrometry|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|date=12 July 2013|volume=24|issue=8|pages=1157–1160|doi=10.1007/s13361-013-0688-8|pmid=23846246|bibcode=2013JASMS..24.1157E|s2cid=6617252}}</ref>
* Eastern Analytical Symposium Award for Outstanding Achievements in Mass Spectrometry, 2014<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catherine Fenselau Awarded 2014 Eastern Analytical Symposium Award for Outstanding Achievements in Mass Spectrometry |url=https://www.asms.org/publications/journal-of-the-american-society-for-mass-spectrometry-group/news-detail/2014/10/29/catherine-fenselau-awarded-2014-eastern-analytical-symposium-award-for-outstanding-achievements-in-mass-spectrometry |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=www.asms.org}}</ref>
* Distinguished Contribution Award,  the Association for Mass Spectrometry and Advances in Clinical Lab (MSACL), 2017<ref>{{Cite web |title=Recognition Awards |url=https://www.msacl.org/index.php?header=MSACL_2023&tab=Recognition_Awards |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=www.msacl.org}}</ref>
* US Human Proteome Organization Catherine E. Costello Lifetime Achievement in Proteomics Award, 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=US HUPO - Lifetime Achievement Award |url=https://www.ushupo.org/Lifetime-Achievement |access-date=2022-06-11 |website=www.ushupo.org}}</ref>
* Fellow of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fellows of ASMS |url=https://www.asms.org/about-asms-awards/fellows-of-asms |access-date=2025-05-18 |website=Default}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Fenselau was married twice, first to Allan H. Fenselau, with whom she had two sons, and later to [[Robert J. Cotter]].<ref name="Obituary">{{cite news|last=Siegel|first=Andrea F.|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2012/11/18/robert-j-cotter-johns-hopkins-medical-school-professor/|title=Robert J. Cotter, Johns Hopkins medical school professor|date=November 18, 2012|newspaper=The Baltimore Sun|access-date=16 March 2014}}</ref><ref name="Windsor">{{cite book|last=Windsor|first=Laura Lynn|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QtZtkf35CF0C&pg=PA76|title=Women in medicine: an encyclopedia|publisher=ABC-Clio|year=2002|isbn=978-1576073926|location=Oxford|pages=76–77}}</ref>
